algorithms.name: RSA
algorithms.description: Widely used for asymmetric key exchange, key encapsulation/transport, and digital signatures.
algorithms.score_rationale: High application-defined prioritization score (95/100) reflects complete exposure to Shor's algorithm on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer.
algorithms.explanation: RSA relies on the computational hardness of factoring large composite integers into prime factors. A sufficiently capable, fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can factor integers in polynomial time O((log N)^3), completely breaking both RSA encryption/key transport and RSA digital signatures.
algorithms.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm for prime factorization efficiently derives private keys from public keys, enabling complete decryption of intercepted traffic and signature forgery.
algorithms.alternative: ML-KEM (NIST FIPS 203) for key establishment/key transport; ML-DSA (NIST FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (NIST FIPS 205) for digital signatures.

algorithms.name: ECDH
algorithms.description: Establishes shared secrets across untrusted channels using elliptic-curve point multiplication.
algorithms.score_rationale: High application-defined prioritization score (95/100) due to complete vulnerability to Shor's discrete logarithm attack and susceptibility to 'harvest now, decrypt later' adversary strategies.
algorithms.explanation: ECDH depends on the difficulty of the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP). Because elliptic curves require relatively small key sizes compared to RSA, a quantum computer requires fewer physical/logical qubits to solve ECDLP with Shor's algorithm, breaking all forward secrecy established with classical ECDH.
algorithms.quantum_threat: Shor's algorithm for discrete logarithms recovers elliptic-curve private keys in polynomial time, compromising session keys and recorded encrypted traffic.
algorithms.alternative: ML-KEM (NIST FIPS 203) for post-quantum key encapsulation; consider hybrid schemes (e.g. X25519 + ML-KEM-768) during transition.

algorithms.name: ECDSA
algorithms.description: Creates compact digital signatures and authenticity guarantees using elliptic-curve cryptography.
algorithms.score_rationale: Application-defined prioritization score (90/100) reflecting that Shor's algorithm permits private key derivation from public keys, enabling arbitrary signature forging once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists.
algorithms.explanation: Like ECDH, ECDSA's mathematical foundation is the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP). Shor's algorithm provides an efficient polynomial-time solution for ECDLP. A quantum adversary can extract the private signing key directly from the public verification key.
algorithms.quantum_threat: Shor's discrete logarithm solver derives the private signing key, permitting retroactive and active forgery of digital certificates, firmware updates, and documents.
algorithms.alternative: ML-DSA (NIST FIPS 204) for general signatures or SLH-DSA (NIST FIPS 205) for high-assurance firmware and root signing.

algorithms.name: AES
algorithms.description: A modern symmetric cipher utilized worldwide to protect bulk data at rest and data in transit.
algorithms.score_rationale: Lower application-defined prioritization score (30/100). AES is immune to Shor's algorithm; Grover's algorithm only provides quadratic speedup, which is effectively mitigated by AES-256.
algorithms.explanation: Symmetric ciphers do not rely on abelian group structure or number-theoretic trapdoors. Shor's algorithm is ineffective against AES. Grover's quantum search algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for unstructured brute-force searches (O(2^(n/2)) operations). This reduces 128-bit keys to 64 bits of security, but leaves AES-256 with 128 bits of quantum security margin.
algorithms.quantum_threat: Grover's algorithm accelerates brute-force search quadratically. While AES-128 is weakened to 64 bits of effective security, AES-256 remains secure with 128 bits of post-quantum work factor.
algorithms.alternative: Ensure deployment uses AES-256 with robust authenticated modes (e.g., GCM) and sound quantum-safe key exchange.

algorithms.name: ML-KEM
algorithms.description: The standardized module-lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber.
algorithms.score_rationale: Low application-defined prioritization score (10/100). Fully standardized and designed to resist both classical and quantum algorithmic attacks.
algorithms.explanation: ML-KEM is built on the hardness of the Module Learning With Errors (M-LWE) problem over algebraic lattices. Decades of quantum algorithm research have found no polynomial-time quantum algorithm to solve lattice shortest vector or learning with errors problems.
algorithms.quantum_threat: No known practical quantum or classical attack against the standardized parameter sets (ML-KEM-512, 768, 1024) when implemented with side-channel countermeasures.
algorithms.alternative: No replacement required; implement parameter set ML-KEM-768 (Security Category 3) or ML-KEM-1024 (Category 5) per NIST FIPS 203.

algorithms.name: ML-DSA
algorithms.description: The standardized module-lattice-based digital signature algorithm derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium.
algorithms.score_rationale: Low application-defined prioritization score (10/100). Formally standardized primary digital signature algorithm for general post-quantum cryptography.
algorithms.explanation: ML-DSA is based on the hardness of the Module Learning with Errors (M-LWE) and Module Short Integer Solution (M-SIS) problems in module lattices. It does not possess the algebraic periodicity exploited by quantum Fourier transforms.
algorithms.quantum_threat: No practical quantum attack is known against M-LWE/M-SIS under standardized parameters. Note: as with all cryptosystems, implementation must guard against classical side-channel and fault attacks.
algorithms.alternative: No replacement required; select ML-DSA-65 (NIST Security Category 3) or ML-DSA-87 (Category 5) per NIST FIPS 204.

algorithms.name: SLH-DSA
algorithms.description: A conservative, stateless hash-based digital signature scheme derived from SPHINCS+.
algorithms.score_rationale: Lowest application-defined prioritization score (5/100). Relies on conservative cryptographic hash assumptions with no lattice vulnerability risks.
algorithms.explanation: SLH-DSA relies solely on the security properties of standard cryptographic hash functions (preimage, second-preimage, and collision resistance). Because it relies on minimal mathematical assumptions, it serves as an essential hedge against potential future algebraic breakthroughs in lattice cryptography.
algorithms.quantum_threat: Quantum computers accelerate hash preimage searches quadratically via Grover's algorithm. SLH-DSA parameter sets (e.g. SLH-DSA-128s, 256f) explicitly account for quantum search bounds.
algorithms.alternative: No replacement required; ideal for root certificates and firmware signing where signature verification is fast and larger signature bytes are tolerable.

algorithms.name: CRYSTALS-Kyber (Legacy / Pre-Standard)
algorithms.description: The Round 3 NIST PQC candidate algorithm that was refined and finalized into NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM).
algorithms.score_rationale: Moderate application-defined prioritization score (45/100) due to interoperability and standard compliance debt. Not quantum-vulnerable, but draft implementations diverge from final FIPS 203.
algorithms.explanation: CRYSTALS-Kyber is mathematically resistant to quantum attacks. However, it is a pre-standardization specification. In August 2024, NIST released FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), which modified the key derivation function (KDF) domain separators, parameter validations, and encapsulation output formatting. Round 3 Kyber binaries and wire protocols are incompatible with final FIPS 203.
algorithms.quantum_threat: No mathematical quantum vulnerability, but using pre-standard Kyber incurs critical technical debt, lack of FIPS certification, and protocol interoperability failures.
algorithms.alternative: Upgrade from pre-standard Kyber to standardized ML-KEM (NIST FIPS 203).

reference.title: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM - Historical Note)

algorithms.name: CRYSTALS-Dilithium (Legacy / Pre-Standard)
algorithms.description: The Round 3 NIST PQC candidate signature scheme that was refined and standardized as NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA).
algorithms.score_rationale: Moderate application-defined prioritization score (45/100) due to protocol incompatibility with official FIPS 204 standards.
algorithms.explanation: CRYSTALS-Dilithium resists quantum attacks on module lattices. However, NIST's finalized FIPS 204 standard introduced modifications to hashing domain separation, context strings, and key formatting. Pre-standard Dilithium artifacts will not validate under standardized FIPS 204 verifiers.
algorithms.quantum_threat: No known mathematical quantum exploit, but deployment risks include compliance failure, missing FIPS validation, and incompatibility with standard PKI systems.
algorithms.alternative: Upgrade implementations from Round 3 Dilithium to finalized ML-DSA (NIST FIPS 204).

reference.title: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA - Historical Note)

algorithms.name: Falcon (Candidate in Progress)
algorithms.description: A lattice signature based on NTRU with very compact signatures and fast verification, currently being finalized by NIST into the forthcoming FN-DSA standard.
algorithms.score_rationale: Application-defined prioritization score (40/100) reflecting non-standardized status. While quantum-resistant, implementation without final NIST FIPS parameters risks obsolescence.
algorithms.explanation: Falcon provides compact signatures and very fast verification by utilizing Gaussian sampling over NTRU lattices. While selected for standardization, NIST prioritized ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for immediate release in 2024. Falcon's draft standard (designated FN-DSA) is slated for publication in 2025/2026. Constant-time floating-point operations in Falcon also present high implementation complexity.
algorithms.quantum_threat: No mathematical quantum attacks are known against its NTRU lattice foundation. The primary risks are implementation pitfalls (timing attacks in non-constant-time floating-point arithmetic) and lack of a finalized standard.
algorithms.alternative: Deploy standardized ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) today; monitor NIST's upcoming FN-DSA standard if compact signature size is strictly mandatory.
